Grip and handedness are not sourced, so the record leaves them out; nor is where he places the beat (ahead, on top, behind), so feel_profile has no beat_placement.

identity.name: Matt Helders
identity.summary: Arctic Monkeys' drummer from their start in Sheffield in 2002, and their loudest backing voice. He took the drums because the others had the guitars, learned in Alex Turner's garage, and played the first record's fast songs with two hands on the hat in sixteenths and the snare on every beat; Queens of the Stone Age made him hit harder, and rap 'the groove element'. On AM, with a hip-hop beat in mind, the restraint to stomp four on the floor for a whole song. I Bet You Look Good on the Dancefloor, The View from the Afternoon, Brianstorm, Teddy Picker, Fluorescent Adolescent, Crying Lightning, R U Mine?, Do I Wanna Know?, Arabella; then Iggy Pop's Post Pop Depression.

traditions.impact: 'We were rap fans at school more than now ... it still influences us in some ways; like for me, it's the drummin'.' 'The groove element.'

traditions.tradition: Hard rock: Queens of the Stone Age live
traditions.impact: Seeing Queens of the Stone Age at a festival was the biggest influence on his development as a drummer: it made him want to 'start hitting harder'.

formative_events.event: The band formed in High Green with the guitars already taken: 'If I wanted to be in the band it was drums only. So I used to keep them in Alex's garage, and we practiced there.' 'It was a slow start. I just didn't want to be left out.'
His first good kit, a Premier, for his 18th birthday: 'obviously Keith Moon played Premier', and it was made in England.

evidence.note: Quoted from MusicRadar; the year is his 18th birthday, May 2004.

eras.label: The first two records
eras.context: Whatever People Say I Am, That's What I'm Not (2006, Andy Nicholson on bass) and Favourite Worst Nightmare (2007, Nick O'Malley): fast, loud indie rock from Sheffield, made quickly to get back on the road.
defining_traits: two hands on the hat in sixteenths, the snare in its place
the snare on every beat at full tilt

eras.label: Humbug and Suck It and See
eras.context: Humbug with Josh Homme in the desert (2009), then Suck It and See (2011): slower, heavier and darker.
defining_traits: a chorus built up from the snare alone
eras.style_shift: From fast indie rock to heavier, slower grooves under Josh Homme.

eras.label: AM
eras.context: AM (2013), recorded bass and drums first for the groove, with a 'Dr. Dre beat' in mind; the London Olympics opening ceremony (2012) and Glastonbury's Pyramid Stage (2013) on the Union Jack Premier.
defining_traits: four on the floor and nothing else (Do I Wanna Know?)
the kick on the 'a's (R U Mine?)
eras.style_shift: Restraint: the groove under the song rather than the fill.

eras.label: Iggy Pop and the later records
eras.context: Iggy Pop's Post Pop Depression with Josh Homme (2016) and its tour; Lady Gaga's Joanne (2016); Tranquility Base Hotel & Casino (2018) and The Car (2022), where 'restraint' is the word he uses; Terrific with Tyler Parkford (2025).

genres.notes: An influence on the groove ('for me, it's the drummin''), not a genre he records in.

swing.notes: Straight eighths and sixteenths in every tab read.

dynamics.balance: Hit hard ('start hitting harder'); few ghost notes in the tabs, a handful in R U Mine?'s chorus.

feel_profile.interaction: Locks the kick to the riff (Brianstorm, R U Mine?) and lets the hat and the snare share sixteenths between two hands; the loudest backing vocal in the band, singing over his own playing.

hand_techniques.name: Two hands on the hat in sixteenths
hand_techniques.description: The hat in sixteenths with both hands, the snare in the hat's place on the backbeat and its pickups: The View from the Afternoon's verse, Brianstorm's verse, Teddy Picker's solo.

hand_techniques.name: The snare on every beat
hand_techniques.description: The snare on every beat with four on the floor at 207 (I Bet You Look Good on the Dancefloor) and by turns with the backbeat (Teddy Picker's chorus).

hand_techniques.name: Toms round the snare
hand_techniques.description: The high and the floor tom in sixteenths between the backbeats over the kick and the hat foot on every beat (Brianstorm); eighths on the floor tom under the snare (The View from the Afternoon's intro).

foot_techniques.name: The kick with the riff
foot_techniques.description: The kick doubling the guitar riff on the 'a's and 'and's (Brianstorm, R U Mine?), or four on the floor (Do I Wanna Know?); two kicks in a row on 1 in Arabella.

foot_techniques.name: The hat foot in eighths
foot_techniques.description: The hat foot in eighths alone under the crash and the toms (Arabella's pre-chorus), or on every beat under the toms (Brianstorm).

devices_search.note: None found. Brianstorm's breakdown puts the snare, the floor tom and the kick together three, three and two sixteenths apart, a grouping of the bar with no pulse against it; Fluorescent Adolescent's and Arabella's tom bars have triplets in them, a fill's figure. No source describes a polyrhythm in his playing.

voice_language.snare: Backbeat on 2 and 4, often with a pickup on the 'a' of 2; on every beat at full tilt; on the 'and's under open hats (The View from the Afternoon's chorus); runs in fills.
voice_language.kick: With the riff, on the 'a's and 'and's; four on the floor in the fast choruses and in Do I Wanna Know?.
voice_language.toms: The high and the floor tom in sixteenths round the snare (Brianstorm); eighths on the floor tom (The View from the Afternoon); fills down the toms.
voice_language.hihat: Sixteenths with two hands, the snare taking a stroke; eighths, opened on the 'and' of 4; open in eighths (R U Mine?); quarters (Arabella); the foot in eighths alone.
voice_language.cymbals: The crash on every beat in a bridge or a chorus (The View from the Afternoon, Arabella), the second crash ridden on 2, 3 and 4 (Do I Wanna Know?), the crash in eighths (R U Mine?'s last chorus).

sound_profile.cymbal_character: Zildjian: K Custom Session hats, K Sweet crashes and a K Light ride on the R U Mine? video kit.

by_era.description: Premier, made in England, 22-, 13- and 16-inch, played hard in small studios.
The Union Jack Premier, 24-, 14- and 18-inch, 'the first bigger kit'; on AM the kit set up in unusual ways for each sound, recorded with the bass first.
A Ludwig Classic Oak in Black Satin, a copper snare, Zildjian Ks.

sample_hints.00s: A loose, rattling British kit, played hard, with a trashy crash.
sample_hints.10s: A dry, close, tight kit, the kick fat and short, for AM.

signature_traits.label: Two hands on the hat
signature_traits.description: The hat in sixteenths with both hands, the snare taking the hat's stroke on 2, the 'a' of 2 and 4: fast indie rock with a funk player's hands.

signature_traits.label: The snare on every beat at full tilt
signature_traits.description: Four on the floor and the snare on every beat at 207 (I Bet You Look Good on the Dancefloor); the snare on every beat in the chorus (Teddy Picker).

signature_traits.label: The toms round the snare
signature_traits.description: Brianstorm: the high and the floor tom in sixteenths between the backbeats over four on the floor.

signature_traits.label: Restraint
signature_traits.description: 'I think it's good when you leave something out.' Do I Wanna Know? is the kick on every beat and the snare on 2 and 4 for the whole song; 'Not everybody can play a simple groove for three minutes with no variation and have it mean something.'

equipment.label: Premier in the Union Jack
equipment.layout_notes: Made in England, 'the first bigger kit that I've got', played at the London Olympics opening ceremony (27 July 2012) and toured after it.

philosophy.idea: Leave something out: restraint is hard for a drummer, and the groove for the song matters more than the fill.
Play to the song: a simple groove held for three minutes, and made to mean something, is harder than it sounds.

The Guardian on Favourite Worst Nightmare: 'if you removed everything from the album except Matt Helders' drumming, it would still be a pretty gripping listen.'
